C1.quote: In L, all objects that can be named are said to be "first class."
C1.statement: Give every nameable thing equal status, assignable, passable and storable, rather than privileging some kinds of object. (instead of: privileged built-ins that can't be passed or stored like ordinary values)

C2.quote: I decided that there should be no undefined result values in L – instead, exceptions should always be raised when no correct return value can be computed.
C2.statement: When no correct value can be computed, raise rather than return an undefined or silently clipped result, and reject inconsistent constructions outright. (instead of: silent sentinels, truncation or undefined behavior as in C)

C3.quote: One of the rules I took from the predecessor was that every data type, when printed or converted to a string, should be represented by an expression that was a valid input to the language's parser.
C3.statement: Make a value's printed form a valid expression that reconstructs it, rather than a free-form description. (instead of: arbitrary, unparseable string descriptions of objects)

C4.quote: Using / 0-based indexing, half-open intervals, and suitable defaults (as L / ended up having), they are beautiful: a[:n] and a[i:i+n]
C4.statement: Index from zero with half-open intervals and suitable defaults so adjacent slices meet without off-by-one corrections. (instead of: 1-based closed intervals needing +1/-1 adjustments)

C5.quote: With explicit references, there is no need to have a special syntax for method definitions nor do you have to worry about complicated semantics concerning variable lookup. Instead, one simply defines a function whose first argument corresponds to the instance, which by convention is named "self."
C5.statement: Make the instance an explicit first argument and explicit attribute access the only way to reach its state, rather than implicit resolution. (instead of: implicit this and hidden instance-variable lookup as in C++)

C6.quote: I decided to generalize these to a common concept, the sequence. This generalization made it so certain core operations such as getting the length (len(s)), indexing (s[i]), slicing (s[i:j]), and iteration (for i in s) worked the same on any sequence type.
C6.statement: Generalize related types under a shared concept so the same core operations work uniformly across them, rather than per-type operations. (instead of: separate, incompatible operations for each container type)

C7.quote: A major design constraint was that I didn't want to add syntax for methods that differed from the syntax for functions. Refactoring the grammar and the byte code generator to handle such similar cases differently felt like a huge task.
C7.statement: Prefer the minimal solution that reuses existing syntax over introducing new syntax for a new feature. (instead of: adding dedicated grammar for each new capability)
